content: The interventions within school health services (SHS) are categorized based on their area, type of health activity, and their final ranking by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) as either essential or suitable, depending on the location. While many interventions could fit into multiple categories, each intervention is assigned to a single category for clarity. For brevity, summary names of interventions are used in the matrix, with full and precise names provided in Web Annex H (Menu of interventions with WHO sources) and Web Annex A (Compendium of interventions with WHO evidence), which offer detailed information about each intervention. The GDG identified 87 interventions as essential or suitable for SHS, organized by type of health service activity and WHO source. These include health promotion, health education, screening, immunizations, clinical assessments, and health services management. For example: 1. Health Promotion: Activities include promoting timely care-seeking, health literacy, personal hygiene, oral health, reduced sugar consumption, physical activity, adequate sleep, and menstrual hygiene management. These interventions are supported by varying levels of WHO guidance. 2. Health Education: This includes providing education on nutrition, sexual and reproductive health, and injury prevention. Full WHO support is available for many of these interventions. 3. Screening and Referral: Screening activities include identifying vision, hearing, oral health, and developmental issues, as well as conditions like anemia, malnutrition, and obesity. Referrals for conditions such as asthma, diabetes, and mental health concerns are also included. 4. Immunizations: Essential vaccines include those for diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B, HPV, measles, and rubella. Mass drug administration for diseases like malaria and helminths is also supported. 5. Clinical Assessments: These involve evaluating adolescent risk behaviors, managing acute and chronic conditions, and providing counseling on topics like nutrition, physical activity, and substance use. 6. Health Services Management: This includes using data for planning and monitoring SHS, as well as ensuring service delivery during emergencies. The GDG also identified seven interventions as unsuitable for inclusion in SHS. Some of these, such as universal screening for maltreatment or intimate partner violence, are not recommended by WHO for any healthcare setting. Others, like screening for hypertension or scoliosis, lack explicit WHO guidance. The WHO guideline on SHS is being disseminated globally through printed publications, online resources, and partnerships with ministries of health and education, universities, and NGOs. Digital technology is being explored to support dissemination and implementation, including telemedicine, health record management, and training for healthcare providers. National adaptation of the guideline is encouraged, with WHO regional and country offices available to assist. SHS programs should align with broader national health strategies, leveraging existing programs and improving them to be more comprehensive and evidence-based. Collaboration between the health and education sectors is critical for effective implementation. The primary beneficiaries of SHS are students, but families and communities also play a role in informing and monitoring these services. SHS can be delivered through school-based or school-linked models, involving trained health workers who collaborate with educators and other sectors to provide comprehensive care.
